claims.claim: PySpark 4.0.4 error texts: UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION with SQLSTATE 42703; CAST_INVALID_INPUT with SQLSTATE 22018 and an origin line; PythonException wrapping a Python traceback; NOT_COLUMN_OR_STR for a generator passed to shadowed sum; getCondition() and getSqlState() on AnalysisException; Column.try_cast exists.
ANSI mode is enabled by default in Apache Spark 4.0 and Databricks Runtime 17.0 and above.
SQLSTATE class 22 is data exception; class 42 is syntax error or access rule violation.

concept_html:
A Spark error message is long, but it has a fixed shape. In PySpark 4.0 (Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS) most errors start with an error condition in square brackets and end with a SQLSTATE:

[UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column, variable, or function
parameter with name `final_wieght` cannot be resolved. Did you mean one
of the following? [`final_weight`, `age`, `wave_id`, `respondent_id`].
SQLSTATE: 42703

Read three things:

  • The condition names the problem. Search for it in the Databricks error conditions reference.
  • The SQLSTATE class, its first two characters. Class 42 is a syntax error or access rule violation: your code names something that does not exist. Class 22 is a data exception: the code is valid but a value is not.
  • The origin line. Runtime errors show == DataFrame == and "cast" was called from ... with your file and line.

When the error appears. Transformations are lazy, so a data error appears at the action (collect, count, write), not at the line that caused it. The origin line points you back. In classic Spark, a missing column fails at once, when you call select.

Python UDF errors arrive as PythonException wrapping a normal Python traceback. Read that inner traceback bottom up (lesson D1-L1).

Shadowed built-ins give a misleading message. Your data_contracts.py imports sum from pyspark.sql.functions. Then sum(1 for c in checks) raises [NOT_COLUMN_OR_STR] Argumentcolshould be a Column or str, got generator. The code never meant to call Spark. Import functions as F.

ANSI mode is on by default in Spark 4.0 and Databricks Runtime 17.0 and above. A cast of 'abc' to INT now raises [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] instead of returning null. Use try_cast where bad values are expected, and count the nulls it produces.

In code, catch pyspark.errors.AnalysisException and read err.getCondition() and err.getSqlState(), not the message text.

Then classify by the SQLSTATE at the end (`SQLSTATE: 42703`): class `"42"` gives `"code"`, class `"22"` gives `"data"`, anything else or no SQLSTATE gives `"unknown"`.

Then classify by the SQLSTATE at the end (SQLSTATE: 42703): class "42" gives "code", class "22" gives "data", anything else or no SQLSTATE gives "unknown".
exercises.solution:
import re

CONDITION_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^\s*\[([A-Z0-9_.]+)\]")
SQLSTATE_PATTERN = re.compile(r"SQLSTATE:\s*([0-9A-Z]{5})")
CLASS_LABELS = {"42": "code", "22": "data"}


def triage(message: str) -> tuple[str | None, str]:
    """Error condition and a first-pass category for a Spark error message.

    Args:
        message: The error message text.

    Returns:
        (condition or None, "code", "data" or "unknown").
    """
    condition_match = CONDITION_PATTERN.match(message)
    condition = condition_match.group(1) if condition_match else None
    state_match = SQLSTATE_PATTERN.search(message)
    if state_match is None:
        return condition, "unknown"
    return condition, CLASS_LABELS.get(state_match.group(1)[:2], "unknown")

title: Spark errors, the condition and the real cause
why_html: After a runtime upgrade to Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS, a silver job that had run for two years failed with [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value 'n/a' ... cannot be cast to "INT". The engineer's first thought was a Spark bug. The SQLSTATE started with 22, a data exception: the data had always held 'n/a', and the old runtime had turned it into null without a word. The new error exposed a data quality problem that was two years old.
